1	# SUBMISSION
     2	
     3	<!-- Fill in every section. The AI Jury studies this file together with the code, the Build Report, the presentation and the Stand's interface. Accepted languages: English, Kazakh, Russian. These hint comments may be deleted. -->
     4	
     5	
     6	## Concept
     7	
     8	
     9	**Enterprise:** OilGuard AI — a digital twin of a fictional onshore oil production field inspired by oil-producing facilities in western Kazakhstan. The implemented model focuses on three production wells and their pressure, temperature and vibration measurements.
    10	
    11	**Users:** Oil field operators, production engineers, maintenance teams and industrial safety specialists.
    12	
    13	**Decision:** The digital twin helps operators decide when to reduce production, stop potentially dangerous equipment, inspect a pipeline or schedule preventive maintenance. The current prototype detects abnormal pressure, temperature and vibration using fixed thresholds. Operational risk prediction and corrective-action comparison are future development goals.
    14	
    15	**Why this choice:** Oil and gas production involves interconnected equipment where failures may cause environmental damage, production losses and safety incidents. A digital twin makes these relationships visible and allows operators to test emergency scenarios without endangering real equipment. The current OilGuard AI prototype combines synthetic telemetry simulation, threshold-based safety detection and local visualization.
    16	
    17	**Real or fictional:** The field is fictional and inspired by onshore oil production facilities in Kazakhstan, including the general operating characteristics of mature oil fields in the Mangystau region. All initial measurements and operating conditions are synthetic. Numerical parameters will be documented as engineering assumptions or supported by publicly available technical references where possible. The project does not claim access to confidential field data.
    18	## Team
    19	
    20	<!-- GitHub usernames of the Participants. Other personal data are not required: the repository becomes public after the Freeze (Rules, section 15). -->
    21	
    22	| GitHub |
    23	|---|
    24	| erasylturgengul |
    25	
    26	## Mine
    27	
    28	OilGuard AI represents a fictional onshore oil production field in western Kazakhstan.
    29	
    30	The digital twin model contains four objects:
    31	
    32	- **oilfield-01:** Parent object representing the oil field.
    33	- **WELL-01:** Production well with pressure, temperature and vibration monitoring.
    34	- **WELL-02:** Production well with a simulated abnormal-pressure incident.
    35	- **WELL-03:** Production well operating under normal conditions.
    36	
    37	All three wells are linked to the parent oil field through the `_parents` attribute.
    38	
    39	Twin definitions: `oilguard_twins.json`.
    40	
    41	Twin generation: `create_oilguard_twins.py`.
    42	
    43	Simulation: `oilguard_simulator.py`.
    44	
    45	MQTT telemetry preparation: `oilguard_mqtt.py`.
    46	
    47	The twins are defined locally but have not yet been verified on a running OpenEgiz Stand.
    48	
    49	## Modules and What-if Scenarios
    50	
    51	OilGuard AI currently provides local simulation and rule-based safety monitoring.
    52	
    53	| Module or What-if Scenario | What it does | How to see it on the Stand | How to undo it (scenarios) |
    54	|---|---|---|---|
    55	| Well monitoring | Simulates pressure, temperature and vibration for three production wells. | Not yet deployed; local CSV and chart are available. | Not applicable |
    56	| Safety detection | Assigns NORMAL or DANGER based on defined sensor thresholds. | Verified locally using MQTT dry-run output. | Not applicable |
    57	| High-pressure incident | Simulates an abnormal operating period for WELL-02 between minutes 70 and 90. | Visible in oilguard_chart.png; not yet controllable on the Stand. | Regenerate the baseline simulation |
    58	
    59	Current detection thresholds:
    60	- Pressure greater than 80 bar.
    61	- Temperature greater than 90 degrees Celsius.
    62	- Vibration greater than 7 mm/s.
    63	
    64	These thresholds are illustrative simulation assumptions, not certified industrial safety limits.
    65	
    66	Interactive What-if controls on the OpenEgiz Stand are planned but not yet implemented.
    67	
    68	## What works and what does not
    69	
    70	### Verified locally
    71	- Python simulation generates 360 telemetry records for three wells.
    72	- The simulation includes 21 DANGER records for WELL-02.
    73	- Pressure monitoring chart is generated successfully.
    74	- Four digital twin definitions are generated in JSON.
    75	- MQTT messages follow the Ditto modify-features structure.
    76	- NORMAL and DANGER messages were verified using dry-run mode.
    77	
    78	### Not yet verified
    79	- Registration of the twins in a running OpenEgiz Stand.
    80	- Live MQTT delivery to the platform.
    81	- Grafana dashboard integration.
    82	- Interactive What-if controls.
    83	
    84	## Data and Assumptions
    85	
    86	All measurements are synthetic and generated using Python.
    87	
    88	Dataset: `oilguard_data.csv`.
    89	
    90	Generator: `oilguard_simulator.py`.
    91	
    92	The dataset contains:
    93	- Three production wells.
    94	- 120 simulated minutes.
    95	- 360 telemetry records.
    96	- Pressure in bar.
    97	- Temperature in degrees Celsius.
    98	- Vibration in mm/s.
    99	- NORMAL and DANGER status labels.
   100	
   101	A high-risk incident is simulated for WELL-02 during minutes 70 through 90.
   102	
   103	The random seed is 42, making the generated dataset reproducible.
   104	
   105	Safety thresholds are illustrative engineering assumptions:
   106	- Pressure > 80 bar.
   107	- Temperature > 90 C.
   108	- Vibration > 7 mm/s.
   109	
   110	These values are not validated against a specific real-world facility.
   111	
   112	No confidential industrial data or personal information is used.
   113	
   114	## Mine visualization
   115	
   116	OilGuard AI currently provides a local pressure monitoring chart.
   117	
   118	Visualization file: `oilguard_chart.png`.
   119	
   120	The chart displays:
   121	- Pressure measurements for WELL-02 over 120 simulated minutes.
   122	- A red dashed line marking the 80 bar warning threshold.
   123	- A highlighted abnormal operating period between minutes 70 and 90.
   124	
   125	The chart is generated using `oilguard_chart.py`.
   126	
   127	OpenEgiz Grafana dashboard integration is not yet completed.
   128	There is currently no verified Stand URL for the OilGuard AI visualization.
   129	
   130	## Limitations
   131	
   132	- All sensor measurements are synthetic.
   133	- The current model represents three wells and one parent oil field.
   134	- Pressure, temperature and vibration are simulated independently.
   135	- The model does not yet calculate physical fluid flow or reservoir dynamics.
   136	- Detection uses fixed thresholds rather than a trained machine learning model.
   137	- The high-pressure incident is predefined rather than controlled interactively.
   138	- Live OpenEgiz deployment and Grafana visualization remain unverified.
   139	- The model is a demonstration and must not be used for real industrial safety decisions.
   140	
   141	## Presentation
   142	
   143	`presentation.pdf` is available in the repository root. No video submitted.
   144	
   145	---
   146	
   147	Platform: OpenEgiz v1.0.4.
   148	
   149	## OilGuard AI Platform Integration
   150	
   151	OilGuard AI includes a Docker Compose integration for OpenEgiz.
   152	
   153	- Digital twins: three oil wells and one parent oil field.
   154	- MQTT simulator: continuously publishes synthetic telemetry.
   155	- Safety monitoring: detects abnormal pressure, temperature and vibration.
   156	- Grafana dashboard: three panels for WELL-02 measurements.
   157	- What-if scenario: simulated abnormal operating conditions at WELL-02.
   158	
   159	### Implementation files
   160	
   161	- `examples/oilguard/compose.yml`
   162	- `examples/oilguard/Dockerfile`
   163	- `examples/oilguard/setup_twins.py`
   164	- `examples/oilguard/twins.json`
   165	- `examples/oilguard/oilguard_mqtt.py`
   166	- `examples/oilguard/dashboard.json`
   167	
   168	### Verification status
   169	
   170	Python syntax, MQTT dry-run and Docker Compose configuration have been verified locally.
   171	
   172	Full deployment on a running OpenEgiz Stand, live MQTT delivery and Grafana data visualization have not yet been verified.

     1	﻿import argparse
     2	import csv
     3	import json
     4	import time
     5	from pathlib import Path
     6	
     7	NAMESPACE = "org.openegiz.oilguard"
     8	
     9	
    10	def make_message(well, row):
    11	    return {
    12	        "topic": f"{NAMESPACE}/{well}/things/twin/commands/modify",
    13	        "path": "/features",
    14	        "value": {
    15	            "pressure": {
    16	                "properties": {
    17	                    "value": float(row["pressure_bar"]),
    18	                    "unit": "bar"
    19	                }
    20	            },
    21	            "temperature": {
    22	                "properties": {
    23	                    "value": float(row["temperature_c"]),
    24	                    "unit": "C"
    25	                }
    26	            },
    27	            "vibration": {
    28	                "properties": {
    29	                    "value": float(row["vibration_mm_s"]),
    30	                    "unit": "mm/s"
    31	                }
    32	            },
    33	            "status": {
    34	                "properties": {
    35	                    "value": row["status"]
    36	                }
    37	            }
    38	        }
    39	    }
    40	
    41	
    42	def main():
    43	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    44	    parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    45	    parser.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=0)
    46	    parser.add_argument("--mqtt-host", default="localhost")
    47	    parser.add_argument("--mqtt-port", type=int, default=1883)
    48	    parser.add_argument("--interval", type=float, default=2.0)
    49	    args = parser.parse_args()
    50	
    51	    csv_path = Path(__file__).with_name("oilguard_data.csv")
    52	
    53	    if not csv_path.exists():
    54	        print(f"ERROR: CSV file not found: {csv_path}")
    55	        return
    56	
    57	    client = None
    58	
    59	    try:
    60	        if not args.dry_run:
    61	            import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
    62	
    63	            client = mqtt.Client(
    64	                mqtt.CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2,
    65	                client_id="oilguard-ai"
    66	            )
    67	            client.connect(args.mqtt_host, args.mqtt_port)
    68	            client.loop_start()
    69	
    70	        published = 0
    71	
    72	        while True:
    73	            with open(csv_path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
    74	                reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    75	                rows_in_cycle = 0
    76	
    77	                for row in reader:
    78	                    well = row["well_id"]
    79	                    payload = json.dumps(make_message(well, row))
    80	
    81	                    if args.dry_run:
    82	                        print(payload)
    83	                    else:
    84	                        client.publish(f"telemetry/{well}", payload, qos=0)
    85	
    86	                        if row["status"] == "DANGER":
    87	                            print(f"ALERT: {well} DANGER", flush=True)
    88	
    89	                        time.sleep(args.interval)
    90	
    91	                    published += 1
    92	                    rows_in_cycle += 1
    93	
    94	                    if args.steps and published >= args.steps:
    95	                        return
    96	
    97	                if rows_in_cycle == 0:
    98	                    print("ERROR: CSV file is empty.")
    99	                    return
   100	
   101	    except KeyboardInterrupt:
   102	        print("Simulator stopped.")
   103	
   104	    finally:
   105	        if client:
   106	            client.loop_stop()
   107	            client.disconnect()
   108	
   109	
   110	if __name__ == "__main__":
   111	    main()

     3	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     4	# Docker Compose deployment (laptops, CI, contest judges): deploy/compose/
     5	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     6	COMPOSE_BASE := docker compose -f deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml
     7	# Once `make example-mine` has run, every compose command also loads the mine
     8	# overlay, so `down` stops its simulator and `up` keeps its Grafana dashboard.
     9	# `make clean` forgets it.
    10	MINE_MARKER  := deploy/compose/.example-mine
    11	MINE_COMPOSE := examples/mine/compose.yml
    12	COMPOSE := $(COMPOSE_BASE)$(if $(wildcard $(MINE_MARKER)), -f $(MINE_COMPOSE))
    13	
    14	## Start the whole platform with Docker Compose (first run: generates credentials)
    15	up:
    16		@bash scripts/compose-env.sh
    17		@bash scripts/compose-preflight.sh
    18		$(COMPOSE) up -d --build --wait --wait-timeout 900
    19		@# `--wait` does not wait for one-shot jobs to finish: a running init counts
    20		@# as up. Wait for it to exit, then check how.
    21		@test "$$(docker wait $$($(COMPOSE) ps -a -q init))" = 0 || { \
    22		  echo "ERROR: the init job (policy + Ditto connections) failed:"; $(COMPOSE) logs init; exit 1; }
    23		@bash scripts/compose-wait-ready.sh
    24		@bash scripts/compose-urls.sh
    25	
    26	## Stop the platform, keep data
    27	down:
    28		$(COMPOSE) down
    29	
    30	## Show compose service status
    31	ps:
    32		@$(COMPOSE) ps -a
    33	
    34	## Follow logs (one service: make logs S=gateway)
    35	logs:
    36		$(COMPOSE) logs -f --tail=100 $(S)
    37	
    38	## End-to-end check of the running compose stack
    39	smoke:
    40		@bash scripts/compose-smoke.sh
    41	
    42	## Run the Example Mine (twins + haul-cycle simulator + Grafana dashboard) on the compose stack
    43	example-mine: up
    44		$(COMPOSE_BASE) -f $(MINE_COMPOSE) up -d --build --wait --wait-timeout 300
    45		@touch $(MINE_MARKER)
    46		@echo "Example Mine running: Grafana -> Dashboards -> OpenEgiz Examples -> Example Mine"
    47	
    48	## Stop the Example Mine simulator (twins and data stay)
    49	example-mine-stop:
    50		$(COMPOSE_BASE) -f $(MINE_COMPOSE) stop mine-simulator
    51	
    52	## Stop the platform and DELETE all its data and credentials
    53	clean:
    54		$(COMPOSE) down -v --remove-orphans
    55		rm -f deploy/compose/.env $(MINE_MARKER)

    57	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    58	# Helm deployment (servers): the chart at the repository root
    59	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    60	# Several values reference names derived from the release name (e.g. the
    61	# telegraf configmap), so the release MUST be called "opentwins" until those
    62	# references are made release-agnostic.
    63	RELEASE_NAME := opentwins
    64	NAMESPACE    := opentwins
    65	CHART_PATH   := .
    66	
    67	# Credentials live OUTSIDE this repo (rotated 2026-08-07). values.yaml carries
    68	# only invalid placeholders, so install/upgrade must always be given this
    69	# override file. Deliberately a hard failure rather than a silent fallback:
    70	# deploying the placeholders would break Ditto auth and telemetry ingest.
    71	SECRETS_FILE ?= $(HOME)/openegiz-deploy/secrets.values.yaml
    72	
    73	# Address browsers use to reach this host; the Grafana app plugin calls Ditto
    74	# and the extended API from the browser. Defaults to the first node's
    75	# InternalIP; override with `make install PUBLIC_HOST=my-host.example`.
    76	PUBLIC_HOST ?= $(shell kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}' 2>/dev/null)
    77	
    78	check-public-host:
    79		@test -n "$(PUBLIC_HOST)" || { \
    80		  echo "ERROR: could not determine PUBLIC_HOST from kubectl."; \
    81		  echo "       Pass it explicitly: make install PUBLIC_HOST=<ip-or-hostname>"; \
    82		  exit 1; }
    83	
    84	check-secrets:

    86		  echo "ERROR: secrets override not found: $(SECRETS_FILE)"; \
    87		  echo "       It holds the Ditto/Grafana/InfluxDB credentials that are"; \
    88		  echo "       intentionally absent from values.yaml. Create it from"; \
    89		  echo "       secrets.values.yaml.example, or point to another file with:"; \
    90		  echo "       make install SECRETS_FILE=/path/to/file"; \
    91		  exit 1; }
    92	
    93	## Install the OpenEgiz Helm chart
